transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-24
Time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 1:03
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (CTO, Cerulean Biome), Sarah Kim (ML Engineer), Raj Patel (Infra), Emily Zhao (Security)

Summary:
Initial migration/discovery call. Cerulean Biome is evaluating options to move away from a mixed vendor stack (Anthropic + in-house vLLM for edge) toward a more unified serving strategy. Primary concerns: inference parity vs their current models, quantization compatibility (INT8/4-bit), latency SLOs for interactive product, and security/KMS for PII-sensitive logs. They want Hosted for quick testing but may need Dedicated or Private for compliance and predictable latency.

Topics covered:
- Current stack and pain points
- Model portability (OpenAI/Anthropic API compatibility, exports from TGI/vLLM)
- Quantization and eval parity
- Hosting modes: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem)
- Security requirements: SOC2, KMS, RBAC, audit logs
- Next steps and benchmarking

[00:00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call, i am alex from redwood, priya is our se, um we can kick off with a short overview from you tom on what you all are trying to solve
[00:00:14] Tom: yeah thanks alex, hey folks, tom here. so high level we're moving from a hybrid approach. we've been using Anthropic Claude via their api for chat flows, but for larger context workloads we run a homegrown vLM stack, sorry vee-ell-em, it's our in-house vLLM fork running on k8s, and it's been a bit brittle, ops heavy, and costy. we're exploring whether we should consolidate to redwood hosted or go for dedicated capacity, maybe private for some regulated clients
[00:00:45] Sarah: and to add, we have subtle quality differences between Claude and our internal models. sometimes prompts that work on Anthropic degrade on vLLM due to tokenization/formatting differences, so parity is a big deal for us. also quantization: some folks tried int8 and got hallucination spikes
[00:01:10] Priya: got it, thanks. when you say "quantization" are you referring to post-training quantization on the model weights or runtime kernel quantization? different knobs there, we have support across a few quant formats but the evaluation can differ
[00:01:23] Sarah: mostly post-train q configs, like 4-bit qlora style, also int8 for inference cost savings. our biggest fear is degrading chat quality during peak interactive flows
[00:01:36] Raj: ops question: what does the switching look like? our infra team needs predictable throughput — p95 latency under 350ms for single-turn chat at 512 tokens is the ask. Also network egress/residency, some customers demand EU data residency
[00:01:51] Alex: fair. That's where Dedicated or Private come in. Dedicated gives isolated GPU pools with predictable throughput and pricing commitments. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you control over data residency and KMS integration. For hosted we can offer region pinning but it's shared capacity so tail latency is a bit more variable
[00:02:10] Emily: from security perspective we need SOC2, SSO (SAML/Okta), key rotation via KMS, and show us audit trails with immutable logs. also curious about how cached KV data is stored and whether we can purge per-tenant
[00:02:25] Priya: on KV caching, our runtime supports prefix and KV cache controls per route. we can honor per-tenant cache isolation and TTL-based purges, and we integrate with customer KMS for encryption at rest for dedicated/private. hosted can use redwood-managed keys or customer-managed keys for enterprise plans
[00:02:44] Tom: practical: latency vs cost. our product needs sub-400ms p95 and we do ~200 qps bursts during peak. can redwood hit that on hosted? or is dedicated required?
[00:02:58] Priya: short answer: depends on model/seq length and batch settings. for interactive low-latency we recommend smaller quantized variants or model distillation. we have throughput profiles for MPT-30B and Llama-2 variants. hosted with burst capacity might get close but to guarantee p95 you usually want Dedicated with pinned GPUs and autoscaling policies
[00:03:20] Sarah: can we port our vLLM checkpoints directly? we want to preserve the fine-tuning from our internal pipelines which are in HF format with some custom kernels
[00:03:34] Alex: we support common HF checkpoints and can import weights; there are sometimes transforms needed for custom kernel ops. priya can follow up on compatibility checklists for TGI/vLLM exports
[00:03:47] Priya: yeah the usual issues are custom attention ops or fused kernels. we have tooling to rewrite or emulate ops, and if it's just a standard transformer with kv cache we can usually onboard it. sometimes we recommend a tiny recompile or a conversion step to our runtime format
[00:04:05] Raj: and GPU flavor? we run a mix of A100s and H100s. will redwood require specific hw? and how does quantization map across hw?
[00:04:18] Priya: our runtime supports both but kernel selection differs. H100 often gets better throughput for longer sequences. quant quantization—excuse me—quantized kernels are different: some int8 kernels are optimized on Ampere/Hopper families; 4-bit kernels sometimes rely on software emulation. we'll include recommended hw+quant matrix in the docs
[00:04:39] Tom: what's the onboarding timeline if we wanted to pilot? we want a quick check — 2 week pilot ideally to validate parity and latency
[00:04:49] Alex: two weeks is realistic for a hosted pilot with a defined prompt set. for dedicated it's longer, usually 4–6 weeks to provision and tune, but we can do a hybrid: start hosted pilot then move to dedicated for production
[00:05:02] Sarah: about eval parity — will redwood run our prompts against both the Anthropic API and our vLLM baseline and show diff reports? we need side-by-side output comparison and metrics for answer quality, helpfulness, toxicity etc
[00:05:16] Priya: yes we have an eval harness that accepts prompt sets and computes metrics. we also can integrate with your eval infra if you have it. sometimes the tokenization differences cause mismatch in outputs; we annotate that in the report and show where formatting or special tokens differ
[00:05:33] Tom: one of our blockers: some prompts rely on proprietary tool-calling and structured outputs. does redwood support function calls and structured schemas out of the box?
[00:05:45] Alex: yes, we support function/tool calling and structured JSON output. we can map your tool interface and provide deterministic fallback behavior. priya can show the schema mapping later in the parity workshop
[00:05:57] [00:06:00] Speaker 1: (crosstalk) okay
[00:06:15] Raj: also curious about cost math: if we use quantized models on dedicated, how much saving vs hosted? ballpark numbers fine
[00:06:25] Priya: typical savings vary a lot: quantizing to 4-bit can reduce inference cost by ~2–4x depending on kernel efficiency and batch. Dedicated changes the unit economics because you commit to capacity so per-token cost drops. we'll send a TCO spreadsheet with math and examples
[00:06:42] Emily: re: compliance, can we get a table of what Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private provides in terms of auditability and legal exposure? ex: data residency guarantees, private keys, on-prem options
[00:06:55] Alex: yes. Hosted = shared infra, support region pinning and enterprise CMKs; Dedicated = isolated GPU pools, stronger SLOs, also CMKs and audit logs; Private = control plane in your VPC or on-prem with full network isolation. we'll include a comparison table in the follow-up
[00:07:12] Tom: you mentioned kernel transforms earlier. what's the risk that a custom vLLM op won't convert and we lose behavior?
[00:07:23] Priya: there's always a small risk. we mitigate by running reference runs before conversion. often custom ops are numeric optimizations; we can offer a shim or fallback to a more generic kernel. if it really depends on a fused op we may need a patch to the model or a small recompile of the vLLM export. we will surface these in a compatibility report
[00:07:42] Sarah: do you support continued quant-aware fine tuning? our team does QLoRA style fine-tunes and we don't want to re-run huge retrains if moving to redwood
[00:07:55] Priya: we support quant-aware inference and also can host fine-tuned artifacts. QLoRA artifacts typically require specific attention to embedding & scaling; we can preserve that in many cases but will validate in the parity run
[00:08:08] [00:08:20] Tom: let's talk risk profile — worst case if outputs change subtly and product regressions happen, how fast can we rollback to current vendor? what's the fallback path?
[00:08:33] Alex: our rollout supports canary deploys and automatic fallback to configured model variants. you can keep Anthropic as a fallback route in a hybrid setup while we ramp. Redwood's smart routing can send traffic by policy (latency, cost, region) and fall back on mismatch conditions
[00:08:50] Raj: observability — we need per-route latency, per-token cost, and traces tied to requests for troubleshooting. do you expose that?
[00:08:59] Priya: yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-route traces, and spans. we can also send logs to your SIEM and support tracing hooks. for Dedicated/Private you can get extended retention windows
[00:09:12] Emily: how do you handle PII in prompts — redaction, storing, retention? for some EU customers we can't persist certain fields longer than 30 days
[00:09:24] Alex: retention is configurable per-tenant. you can choose zero retention for inputs or redact sensitive fields client-side. we support retention TTLs and purge APIs and can sign data processing addenda for EU customers
[00:09:36] Tom: ok good. sample artifacts — can you share the eval harness, sample benchmark spreadsheet and the security whitepaper?
[00:09:45] Alex: yes i'll bundle those: parity harness link, benchmark template, security whitepaper, SOC2 report. priya will follow up on the compatibility checklist. we'll also include an example canary rollout recipe
[00:09:57] Sarah: one quirky issue — our tokenizer outputs special tokens that anthopic handles differently. sometimes truncation leads to context loss. will redwood's tokenizer match ours or will we need conversion middleware?
[00:10:10] Priya: tokenizer mismatches are common. we can normalize tokenization during import or apply a translation layer. we'll flag tokenization diffs in the parity report and propose fixes
[00:10:22] [00:11:00] Tom: timeline recap: hosted pilot in 2 weeks, parity bench within that pilot, then decision to go dedicated or private depending on SLOs/compliance. is that accurate?
[00:11:12] Alex: yes. next step: you share prompt set and traffic profile, priya runs initial parity run, we send pricing + security docs. ideally pilot starts within 10 business days
[00:11:26] Emily: logistics: our procurement needs sample contract terms and data processing addendum in advance of pilot, can you send that?
[00:11:36] Alex: yes i'll include a template and outline of enterprise terms.
[00:11:44] Priya: a quick note on measurements: we'll provide p50/p95/p99 latency, cost per 1k tokens (est), and a similarity/delta metric for output parity. we recommend controlling for random seeds and temperature during parity tests
[00:11:59] Sarah: yep controlling seeds is key. also we'd like to capture hallucination rate measured by a small annotated set
[00:12:10] Alex: great. any other blockers?
[00:12:17] Raj: firewall/egress: if we go private we need to know the ports and IP ranges for provisioning. also VPN or direct connect options
[00:12:27] Priya: we'll include the network requirements. private can be deployed via VPC peering or an on-prem appliance depending on the customer's preference
[00:12:36] Tom: cost question again: do you have a quick example of per-1k-token cost comparing Anthropic + our vLLM ops vs Redwood Dedicated with 4-bit quantization? even rough order of magnitude helps
[00:12:48] Alex: we'll put numbers in the TCO sheet; rough ballpark: if your current blended cost is X, 4-bit on dedicated can halve the per-token spend but remember commit fees change the cashflow. we'll show 3 scenarios: hosted, dedicated (monthly commit), private (capex + ops)
[00:13:05] Emily: security checklist: SOC2, ISO if available, KMS integration, SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, incident response contact — make sure these are in the follow up
[00:13:16] Alex: noted, will include.
[00:13:22] [00:13:45] Priya: ok i'll summarize compatibility risks as: tokenization diffs, custom fused ops, quantization tuning, and runtime kernel mapping. we'll produce a compatibility report with mitigation for each
[00:13:59] Tom: if redwood can show a clean parity run with our prompts and hit p95 < 350ms on dedicated with comparable quality to Anthropic, we'll be comfortable moving forward to pilot commit
[00:14:12] Alex: understood. we'll aim for that.
[00:14:20] Sarah: last tiny thing — will we be able to run incremental A/B with a subset of traffic while keeping the rest on Anthropic?
[00:14:30] Alex: yes, the routing policies support percentage rollouts, canaries, and automatic fallback.
[00:14:38] Emily: and auditability for those rollouts? we need to prove where traffic went historically
[00:14:44] Priya: yes we keep routing traces and you can export them for audits.
[00:14:52] Tom: awesome. let's capture next steps 
[00:14:57] Alex: recap: I'll send docs (pricing, security, contract template), Priya will set up parity harness and run an initial job, Tom will share prompts and traffic profile. we'll sync back in ~1 week and schedule the parity workshop
[00:15:12] Sarah: thanks everyone
[00:15:15] Tom: thanks, talk soon
